Think about what the word currency means - it must link reactions that release energy to reactions that need energy, and be usable immediately.
Recall the chemical change ATP undergoes when it releases energy - what bond is broken and what products are formed?
Remember that a useful currency releases a small, manageable amount of energy per transaction, not a huge burst - what quantity is released per mole?
Consider what must happen after ATP is used up - can the cell remake it easily from ADP, and how often does this happen?

walkthrough:
Why Size and Solubility Matter**
Think of ATP as cash that has to travel. It is a small, water-soluble molecule, so it dissolves in cytoplasm and diffuses quickly from where it is made, for example mitochondria or chloroplasts, to where energy is needed, such as muscles or active transport pumps.

How Energy Is Released in a Usable Packet**
Energy is released by hydrolysis - addition of water breaks off the terminal phosphate group. So $ATP \longrightarrow ADP + Pi + energy$. This releases about $30.5 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$, a small amount that matches the needs of cellular reactions without wasting energy as heat.

Why It Works as a Universal Currency**
Because it gives up energy so easily and immediately, ATP can directly power anabolic and other energy-requiring processes. Catabolic reactions like respiration remake ATP, so ATP sits in the middle, coupling energy-releasing to energy-consuming reactions.

Why It Can Be Used Again and Again**
The ATP to ADP conversion is reversible. ADP + Pi can be re-phosphorylated using energy from respiration or photosynthesis. ATP has a very high turnover - it is constantly broken down and rebuilt, so a small pool can supply a large energy flux.

Final answer: Small and water-soluble so diffuses readily around cell to site of use; immediate energy donor by hydrolysis; removal of terminal phosphate releases $30.5 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$: $ATP \longrightarrow ADP + Pi + energy$; reaction is reversible so ATP can be resynthesised; acts as common intermediate linking energy-yielding and energy-requiring reactions; high turnover, rapidly made and used.

walkthrough:
How the Redox Dye Measures Respiration**
In respiration, hydrogen is released from substrate and normally passed to electron carriers. Methylene blue or DCPIP can act as an artificial hydrogen acceptor. When reduced by gaining hydrogen it changes from blue to colourless, so the faster respiration happens, the faster the blue colour disappears.

Setting Up Anaerobic Yeast Tubes**
Put the same volume and concentration of yeast suspension in each test tube, then add the same volume of sugar solution, for example glucose, plus the same volume of methylene blue solution. To keep conditions anaerobic, cover the mixture with a thin layer of paraffin oil or seal with a bung to prevent oxygen entering, so any dye reduction is due to anaerobic respiration.

Controlling Temperature as the Variable**
Place tubes in thermostatically controlled water baths set to a range of at least five temperatures, for example $10, 20, 30, 40, 50 ^{\circ}C$. Keep all other variables constant: yeast, sugar and dye volumes and concentrations, pH, and time of equilibration before starting the timer.

Measuring Rate and Processing Results**
Start the stopwatch and record time taken for blue colour to disappear completely. For more precision, use a colorimeter to follow decrease in absorbance. Repeat the whole experiment at least twice more at each temperature, calculate mean time, then calculate rate as $1/\text{time}$. Plot rate of respiration against temperature to find optimum and denaturation effect.

Final answer: Methylene blue/DCPIP acts as hydrogen acceptor, decolourised when reduced by respiring yeast. Mix yeast suspension + named sugar solution + dye in tubes, exclude oxygen with oil layer/bung, incubate in water baths at 5+ temperatures. Record time to become colourless or follow with colorimeter. Repeat at least twice more at each temperature, calculate mean, calculate rate as $1/T$, plot rate against temperature.
